messages.subject: MRDS: identifying duplicate sightings
parts:
Dear all,

I am currently undertaking aerial surveys to estimate abundance for commo=
n dolphins in the Hauraki Gulf, New Zealand, using MRDS methods. We are r=
unning into a few issues surrounding how to identify duplicates and recon=
cile differences between duplicate records; in particular how to deal wit=
h differences in group size records between observers.=20

=46rom looking at the literature, I have found that most people have used=
1) timing (within 5 seconds) 2) group size (plus or minus a few individu=
als) 3) angle (plus or minus 5-10 degrees), to identify duplicate sightin=
gs between observers. A sighting was considered a duplicate when two of t=
he three criteria match.

However, for common dolphins, there is huge variation in group size, and =
we often encounter groups that consist of at least ~40 to 300 individuals=
. As a result, most of the time an absolute count of the number of indivi=
duals is not possible and the discrepancy between group size estimates fr=
om two observers can be quite large.=20=20

=46rom the literature, I have found two alternative solutions. The first =
is to use the average group size when there is a difference. The second i=
s to use the larger estimate, under the assumption that under-counting th=
e number of individuals is more likely than over-counting. However, the s=
pecies in these studies typically occurred in small groups and therefore =
differences in counts were by a few individuals, rather than by 10-15 ind=
ividuals (in some cases more) as we have in our study.

A further complication is that individuals within larger groups often for=
m sub-groups that are spatially diffuse. In this case, observers on the s=
ame side of the plane may focus their attention on different sub-groups. =
However, these sub-groups may be of similar size and seen within ~5 secon=
ds but with their centers at different angles. As a result, it doesn't re=
ally make sense to use the standard criteria to identify duplicates.=20

I was wondering if anyone had faced similar problems working on similar s=
pecies, and if so, whether anyone could possibly share their solution wit=
h me?

Kind Regards,
Olivia Hamilton (oham004aucklanduni.ac.nz)
PhD Candidate
Institute of Marine Science
University of Auckland
